title: The Antikythera Mechanism

paragraphs.text: When we talk of the history of computers, most of us will refer to the evolution of the modern digital desktop PC, charting the decades-long developments by giant corporations. What many don't consider, however, is that computers date back millennia. Today, the machine which is sometimes called the world's oldest known 'computer' is the Antikythera mechanism. It is the bronze remains of a clockwork-like piece of technology found by an archaeological dive team at the beginning of the 20th century, in a shipwreck near the Mediterranean island of Antikythera. On the shipwreck were also incredible works of art, jewels and marble statues, and their restoration was understandably prioritised by archaeologists. Because the mysterious bronze object was in such bad condition, it wasn't until the 1970s that its significance was discovered. This was when radiography revealed to researchers that it was in fact a complex mechanism of at least 30 gear wheels.

The mechanism has since been established as the first known astronomical calendar, a complex system which can track and predict the solar system's cycles. Technically, it is in fact a sophisticated mechanical 'calculator' rather than the true computer it is sometimes mistakenly called, since it cannot be reprogrammed, but is nonetheless impressive. Since 2004, an international team has applied modern 3D imaging methods to investigate the mechanism's structure and function. These techniques have now revealed many texts on its surfaces and even much of the writing which became buried inside the remaining fragments, as a result of damage occurring as the ship went down, and which continued as strong ocean currents disturbed the shipwreck over time.

So what do archaeologists now know about the Antikythera mechanism? When first made, it was about the size of a shoe box. A handle on the side enabled users to turn the many gears inside. On the front, pointers showed where the sun and moon were in the sky. On the rear, dials displayed a 19-year cycle of lunar months, and even a four-year cycle of athletic competitions including the Olympic games. The texts have given archaeologists an idea of the pieces of the mechanism that have long since vanished, including a display of tiny spheres that would once have been attached to the pointers and that represented several planets. The texts also include passages about what stars would be bright in the sky or were about to be lost from sight in the glare of the sun at different times of the year. Having examined the wording and expressed issues in these passages, archaeologists have realised they are very close to those in a well-known astronomical text by Greek astronomer Geminos from the first century BC, so presumably the mechanism was also assembled around this time. Geminos is known to have lived on Rhodes, so perhaps the creators of the mechanism lived there too. Lending further support to this theory is a contemporary historic record which mentions other astronomical devices of this type.

Some mysteries remain. For what primary reason was the mechanism built? Was it some kind of teaching device? Would it have had any religious significance? Was it in fact an impressive toy built for the entertainment of someone with high status, as was recently proposed by science writer Jo Marchant in Decoding the Heavens? This last suggestion is seeming less and less likely. This was a serious bit of engineering, with a very detailed astronomical description.

The mechanism is basically an astronomical device, which bears witness both to the ancient Greeks' astronomical knowledge and to their extraordinary, and rather unrecognised, mechanical design skills. One other small detail may hint at its integration into our ancestors' view of the wider world too. Some of the texts seem to be discussing the possible colours of eclipses, which might be interpreted in the context of whether the eclipse was a good or bad sign for the future.

To further understand the Antikythera mechanism, what is really needed are more mechanical devices from the same classical era, or explanatory texts. Unfortunately, the melting down of valuable metal, both in ancient and medieval times, has resulted in nearly all mechanisms being destroyed. Divers still return to the shipwreck, hoping to find pieces that long ago became separated from the device, or perhaps even a second intact mechanism like the only one we have now. But the chances of such a discovery are slim at best.

The Antikythera mechanism is a delicate shell of what it once was. On display at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, its fragility is obvious. Unless extreme caution is taken with objects like this, history can easily turn to dust. In 1953, when the French diver Jacques Cousteau took a team to the site of the shipwreck, they used a net-like piece of equipment to lift up ancient objects. They picked up many artefacts this way, including pottery and wooden planks, but there's no telling what may have been destroyed. Researchers believe that if any of the pieces of the Antikythera mechanism went through that net, they would have disintegrated.

An enticing possibility is that the Antikythera mechanism was on the ship because it was being delivered to a customer. If one device was being delivered, might there be more on other ships that sank after leaving Rhodes? These might help indicate the extent of the spread of geared technology before it almost completely disappeared from view in the rather obscure period that lasted from 500 AD until the sudden blossoming again of gearwork in the era of the medieval cathedral clocks from about 1180 AD, well over a millennium after the Antikythera mechanism.

groups.title: What archaeologists now know about the Antikythera mechanism
content: The mechanism was shoe-box size, and featured a series of dials, a handle, pointers and numerous gears. As well as revealing the movements and events of the solar system, the mechanism indicated when {{32}} would occur. The texts on the mechanism also suggest that certain {{33}} had once corresponded to some planets. Furthermore, archaeologists believe that the mechanism indicated the {{34}} of particular stars during the year. An analysis of the {{35}} found on the mechanism has helped archaeologists establish when it was probably built. There is also evidence that the mechanism might have been built on Rhodes, where an ancient document refers to {{36}} .
